input:
In this work, the rate constant k of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was carefully measured at two different temperatures to characterise how the reaction responds to temperature. At 300 K, k was found to be 0.015 s-1, whereas at the higher temperature of 340 K, k rose substantially to 0.718 s-1. Over the 40 K interval between the measurements, the rate constant increased by a factor of 47.9, highlighting its strong temperature sensitivity.

The value at 340 K is a derived value. It was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 82 kJ mol-1, rather than being measured directly, and the value at 300 K serves as the measured anchor for that computation. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%, which indicates that the reported constants are based on three readings at each temperature rather than on single readings. The 4% figure represents the spread of those triplicate readings around their mean at each temperature, and the derived constant at 340 K effectively carries the same relative spread through the computation, since the computation starts from the measured constant together with the stated activation energy.

Between the two temperatures, a rate constant at an intermediate temperature can also be obtained from the same Arrhenius relation with the same activation energy, although such a value would have the same status as the 340 K constant, namely computed rather than measured. The temperature dependence described is steep, and it is the dependence of the stated reaction in the stated solvent over the stated interval.

The dataset is bounded at the top by the solvent. Above 340 K, the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. The two constants describe the reaction at 300 K and 340 K, with the upper one derived, and they do not extend beyond 340 K, as a value above that temperature would require a sampling method that keeps the solvent in place.

The rate constant k of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.015 s-1. At 340 K, k = 0.718 s-1. Across the 40 K interval between the two measurements, k increases by a factor of 47.9.

The value at 340 K is a derived value. It was computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 82 kJ mol-1 rather than measured directly, and the value at 300 K is the measured anchor for that computation. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. The reported constants therefore rest on three readings at each temperature, not on single readings, and the 4% figure is the spread of those triplicate readings about their mean at each temperature. The derived constant at 340 K carries the same relative spread through the computation, because the computation starts from the measured constant and the stated activation energy.

Between the two temperatures, a rate constant at an intermediate temperature can be obtained from the same Arrhenius relation with the same activation energy. Such a value has the same status as the 340 K constant: computed, not measured. The temperature dependence the pair describes is steep, and it is the dependence of the stated reaction in the stated solvent over the stated interval.

The dataset is bounded at the top by the solvent. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. The two constants describe the reaction at 300 K and 340 K, the upper one derived, and they do not extend past 340 K: a value above that temperature would require a sampling method that holds the solvent in place, and no such measurement stands behind this pair.
